what_it_does: Enterprise servers — the machines that run bank transactions, airline reservations, and similar mission-critical workloads — must deliver consistently fast responses even when heavily loaded, often running at over 90% of their processing capacity with hundreds of virtual machines sharing the same hardware. The cache hierarchy (the series of fast on-chip memory banks — called L1, L2, L3, and so on — that hold recently used data close to the processor cores to avoid expensive trips to main memory) is critical to achieving this. This paper describes the cache design in IBM's Telum and Telum II mainframe processors, which spread the largest cache level across multiple chiplets (separate silicon dies that function as one processor) connected by fast on-chip links, rather than placing it in a single monolithic block. An algorithm dynamically decides which level of this distributed cache hierarchy should hold each piece of hot (frequently accessed) data based on the current workload's behavior, adapting as the workload changes. The Telum II design extends this foundation to also handle generative AI inference workloads alongside traditional enterprise jobs.
